stories.headline: S&P 500 SINKS 4.36%, NASDAQ 100 ENTERS CORRECTION IN WORST AI-DRIVEN SELLOFF SINCE MARCH 2020
stories.body: The S&P 500 fell 4.36% to 7,354 and the Nasdaq 100 dropped 6.36% to 26,630, its worst session since the pandemic crash, erasing all of Wednesday's post-midterm rally in a single day. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index (SOX) plunged roughly 12%, also its worst day since March 2020, as investors dumped AI infrastructure names across the board.
stories.explain: Wednesday's rally priced in reduced policy risk from a clean midterm outcome, but Thursday's reversal shows the market re-pricing a different risk: that a Democratic Congress means tighter scrutiny of AI data-center buildout, power consumption, and antitrust exposure for the hyperscalers funding it. Because so much of the AI trade's valuation sits in cash flows years out, even a modest rise in the perceived odds of slower buildout forces a disproportionately large markdown in present value, which is why the Nasdaq 100 fell nearly 50% more than the S&P 500 on the same day.

stories.headline: CHIP STOCKS LEAD THE ROUT: AMD DROPS 17%, NVIDIA FALLS 9%, QUALCOMM AND ARM SINK ON WEAK OUTLOOKS
stories.body: Advanced Micro Devices fell about 17% and Nvidia dropped roughly 9%, dragging the SOX index down 12%, after Qualcomm and Arm Holdings both issued underwhelming forward guidance in Wednesday-night earnings. Neoclouds CoreWeave and Nebius, which rent out AI compute capacity, slid about 10% and 15% respectively as the selling spread from chipmakers to the infrastructure layer built on top of them.
stories.explain: Qualcomm and Arm's guidance matters less for its own numbers than for what it implies about the next leg of chip demand, since both companies sit upstream of the smartphone and data-center buildout that has anchored the AI trade's growth story. When bellwether suppliers signal decelerating orders, algorithmic and momentum strategies tend to sell the entire supply chain at once rather than wait to confirm the slowdown name by name, which is why the damage cascaded from chipmakers into neoclouds that have no direct earnings link to Qualcomm or Arm.

stories.headline: DEMOCRATIC MIDTERM SWEEP TURNS FROM TAILWIND TO HEADWIND AS INVESTORS PRICE IN AI REGULATION RISK
stories.body: Tuesday's Democratic sweep of the House and a projected 54-44 Senate lifted stocks Wednesday on reduced trade-policy uncertainty, but by Thursday the same result was being read as a threat to the AI buildout, as traders weighed incoming Democratic state governors pausing data-center permits and tighter federal scrutiny of AI power demand. Palantir and CrowdStrike, both widely held AI-adjacent software names, fell more than 10% on the reassessment.
stories.explain: A single election result can carry offsetting implications for different parts of the market, and today's reversal shows the AI-capex trade losing out to the trade-policy relief that drove Wednesday's gain. The mechanism is the same one behind Wednesday's rally, just flipped: traders are repricing the probability that a Democratic Congress constrains a specific growth driver, here data-center permitting and AI oversight, rather than reassessing the economy's near-term fundamentals, which is why the reversal hit AI-linked names far harder than the broader market.

stories.headline: 10-YEAR YIELD SLIPS 6 BPS TO 4.84% AS FLIGHT-TO-SAFETY BID OFFSETS 85% ODDS OF A DEC. 9 HIKE
stories.body: The 10-year Treasury yield eased 6 bps to 4.84% even as CME FedWatch pricing continued to show roughly 85% odds of a quarter-point hike at the Fed's Dec. 9 meeting, as the equity rout drove safe-haven demand for government debt. The move is notable because a rate hike that's still priced at 85% would ordinarily keep yields elevated or rising, not falling.
stories.explain: Treasury yields compensate investors for the expected policy-rate path, inflation, and a term premium for uncertainty, and today's drop shows the flight-to-safety component overwhelming the policy-rate component for one session. A sharp, broad-based equity selloff typically triggers reflexive buying of Treasurys as the default safe asset regardless of what the Fed is expected to do weeks later, so yields can fall even while hike odds hold steady, a divergence that tends to close quickly once the immediate risk-off impulse fades.

stories.headline: OIL JUMPS 5.2% TO $91 ON RENEWED MIDDLE EAST RISK PREMIUM EVEN AS EQUITIES CRATER
stories.body: WTI crude rose 5.24% to about $91 a barrel, a sharp reversal from this week's de-escalation-driven slide, as renewed concern over the durability of any Iran wind-down reintroduced supply-disruption risk into the price. The move is unusual timing-wise, since oil typically falls alongside equities in a broad risk-off session rather than rallying against it.
stories.explain: Oil's price embeds a forward-looking premium for the probability that conflict disrupts flows through chokepoints like the Strait of Hormuz, and that premium can swing in either direction within a single session as headlines shift the market's read on disruption odds, independent of what is happening in equities. Today's rally shows the commodity-specific geopolitical risk channel dominating the macro risk-off channel that would normally pull oil down with stocks, underscoring that crude's 2026 moves have been driven more by headline-to-headline probability repricing than by actual changes in supply or demand.

stories.headline: APPLOVIN SURGES 30% ON EARNINGS, A LONE BRIGHT SPOT AS AI-ADJACENT NAMES ARE SOLD INDISCRIMINATELY
stories.body: AppLovin jumped nearly 30% after beating on both revenue and profit, standing out against a tape where Tesla fell roughly 10% and most AI-linked software and chip names were down double digits regardless of their own fundamentals. Retail investors sold a reported $358 million of equities, their heaviest single-day selling since 2020.
stories.explain: AppLovin's gain against the grain shows that company-specific earnings quality still matters even inside a macro-driven selloff, since its results gave investors a concrete reason to buy rather than a narrative to fear. The broader pattern, heavy, indiscriminate selling across AI-adjacent names regardless of individual balance sheets, is the hallmark of a sentiment-and-positioning-driven unwind rather than a fundamentals-driven repricing, which is also why record retail selling volume is a useful signal: it shows the deleveraging reaching even the buy-the-dip cohort that had been a reliable source of support all year.

watchlist: Nonfarm payrolls Friday, Nov. 6, 8:30 AM ET — October jobs data, first major release after today's AI-driven selloff
CPI release Tuesday, Nov. 10 — last major inflation print before the Dec. 9 FOMC decision
FOMC meeting Dec. 9 — CME FedWatch pricing roughly 85% odds of a quarter-point hike
Remaining Q3 earnings from hyperscalers and chipmakers — watch capex guidance for signs of a genuine AI-spending pullback versus a sentiment-driven overreaction
SOX semiconductor index technical retest after its worst session since March 2020

deepDive.title: Why Chip Stocks Fell 3x Harder Than the Market: Duration Risk in the AI Trade
content: Today's brief centers on a lopsided move: the S&P 500 fell 4.36% while the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index (SOX) plunged roughly 12%, nearly three times the broad market's decline, on the same day and the same news. Nvidia, AMD, CoreWeave, and Nebius, companies with no shared earnings report that day, all fell together, while a company like AppLovin that actually beat estimates rallied 30%. For a finance student, the gap between the index-level move and the chip-sector move is the real story, and it has a precise name: duration risk.

Equity duration works like bond duration, measuring how sensitive a stock's present value is to changes in the discount rate or in the timing of its cash flows. A mature, profitable company earning most of its cash now has low duration; a company whose valuation depends on data-center capacity, power contracts, and chip demand materializing over the next five to ten years has high duration. In a simplified Gordon-growth framing, value equals expected cash flow divided by the discount rate minus the growth rate, so when growth is priced in far out and skewed to the high end, small changes in either the discount rate or the perceived probability of that growth arriving produce outsized swings in present value, exactly the mechanism behind AMD's 17% drop and Nvidia's 9% drop on a single news catalyst.

What's easy to miss is that the trigger here wasn't new legislation; nothing restricting AI data centers has actually been enacted. The move was a probability repricing, the market raising its estimate that a Democratic Congress and incoming state governors will eventually constrain permitting, power use, or antitrust exposure for the hyperscalers funding the buildout. That is structurally similar to 2000, when Cisco fell more than 80% from its peak over the following two years not because its revenue collapsed immediately, but because the market had priced in a growth trajectory that required near-perfect execution for decades, and any doubt about that trajectory forced a severe markdown even while the underlying business kept growing.

That same duration lens explains why Friday's payrolls, next week's CPI, and the Dec. 9 FOMC decision matter disproportionately for chip and AI-infrastructure stocks from here, more than for the index as a whole. Each of those releases feeds directly into the discount-rate assumption embedded in every long-duration AI valuation: a soft jobs number that lowers hike odds would mechanically ease the pressure on exactly the stocks that fell hardest today, while a hot CPI print would compound it. Understanding duration is what lets you separate a stock-specific regulatory scare, which may fade once nothing is actually enacted, from a genuine repricing of the discount rate, which would not.
